blocks.text: 1. Product Quantization

blocks.alt: A vector splits into subvectors, producing compact codes

blocks.text: Product Quantization covers the compression technique in full depth, giving it a complete standalone treatment.
It splits a vector into smaller subvectors and compresses each one separately, producing a compact vector representation.
2. The Promised Full Explanation
IVF-PQ previewed just enough of this technique to explain how it combines with clustering.
This topic gives product quantization the complete, dedicated treatment it deserves.
3. Splitting A Vector Into Subvectors

blocks.alt: A full vector splits into subvector 1 and subvector 2

blocks.text: A long vector gets sliced into several smaller, equal sized chunks.
Each subvector then gets compressed independently of the others.
4. Learning A Codebook Per Subvector

blocks.alt: A subvector space learns a codebook

blocks.text: A small set of representative subvector values, called a codebook, gets learned for each slice.
Every actual subvector then gets replaced by the closest codebook entry's index.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Component","Role"],"rows":[["Subvector","A slice of the original full vector"],["Codebook","A learned set of representative values for that slice"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Storing Codes Instead Of Raw Values

blocks.alt: A raw subvector becomes a small code ID

blocks.text: Instead of storing full precision numbers, only a small integer code per subvector gets stored.
That tiny code represents an entire chunk of the original vector.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A subvector of eight 32 bit floating point numbers can be replaced by a single small integer code, often just one byte, representing that entire slice through its closest codebook entry.

blocks.text: 6. Reconstructing Approximate Distances

blocks.alt: Stored codes go through a codebook lookup to produce an approximate distance

blocks.text: Distances get estimated using precomputed lookup tables built from the codebooks, the same mechanism used for fast approximate distances in IVF-PQ.
This avoids ever reconstructing the full precision vector during search at all.
7. Compression Ratio In Practice

blocks.alt: A full vector at 100 percent is compared against a small PQ code fraction

blocks.text: Splitting into more, smaller subvectors allows for more aggressive compression.
That same aggressiveness trades away more precision, the accuracy loss that comes with any compression.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A vector split into more subvectors achieves a smaller total storage footprint since each individual subvector needs fewer bits to represent, but each smaller slice also captures less of the original signal precisely.

blocks.text: 8. Choosing The Number Of Subvectors
Too few subvectors leave each codebook representing too broad a range of values.
Too many subvectors instead add overhead without proportional accuracy gains.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Subvector count","Effect"],"rows":[["Too few","Each codebook covers too broad a range, losing precision"],["Too many","Diminishing accuracy gains with added overhead"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Product Quantization Is Worth Applying

blocks.alt: A massive vector count points toward using product quantization

blocks.text: Very large collections needing aggressive memory savings benefit most.
Small collections where every bit of accuracy matters may prefer full precision vectors instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates splitting a vector into subvectors and replacing each with a codebook index.

code.content:
import random

def split_into_subvectors(vector, num_subvectors):
    subvector_size = len(vector) // num_subvectors
    return [vector[i:i + subvector_size] for i in range(0, len(vector), subvector_size)]

def build_codebook(subvectors_at_position, codebook_size=4):
    return random.sample(subvectors_at_position, min(codebook_size, len(subvectors_at_position)))

def encode_subvector(subvector, codebook):
    distances = [sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(subvector, code)) for code in codebook]
    return distances.index(min(distances))

original_vector = [round(random.uniform(-1, 1), 3) for _ in range(16)]
subvectors = split_into_subvectors(original_vector, num_subvectors=4)

print(f"Original vector: {original_vector}")
print(f"Split into {len(subvectors)} subvectors: {subvectors}\n")

codebooks = [build_codebook([sv], codebook_size=1) for sv in subvectors]
codes = [encode_subvector(subvectors[i], codebooks[i]) for i in range(len(subvectors))]

print(f"Encoded as small integer codes: {codes}")
print(f"Original storage: {len(original_vector)} floats, Compressed storage: {len(codes)} small integers")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the original sixteen value vector reduced to just four small integer codes, dramatically shrinking storage requirements.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Choosing too few subvectors, leaving codebooks representing an overly broad range of values.
Choosing too many subvectors, adding overhead without meaningful accuracy improvement.
Applying product quantization to a small collection where the accuracy tradeoff outweighs the benefit.
Forgetting that distances become approximate estimates rather than exact calculations after quantization.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Product quantization splits a vector into smaller subvectors and compresses each one separately.
It gives IVF-PQ's previewed compression technique its own complete, dedicated treatment.
A long vector gets sliced into several smaller, equal sized chunks before compression.
A learned codebook of representative values replaces each actual subvector with a small code index.
Storing a small integer code per subvector dramatically reduces storage compared to full precision.
Distances get estimated using precomputed lookup tables, avoiding full vector reconstruction.
More, smaller subvectors allow more aggressive compression at the cost of more precision loss.
Choosing the right number of subvectors balances compression ratio against accuracy.
